beats.intro: Alternative investments, module two. [[sub]]How do you measure the performance of an investment that is illiquid, leveraged, and paid for through complex fees?
beats.why: [[a]]Public stocks and bonds are easy to compare. They are standardized, priced continuously, and have peer groups and indexes. [[alt]]Alternatives are customized. Their cash flows come at uneven times, they may use borrowed money, they are hard to value, and their fees and taxes are complicated. [[four]]Four areas deserve scrutiny: the life cycle of the investment, the use of leverage, the valuation of the assets, and the fee structure. Returns are also usually less normally distributed, so the usual risk measures fit less well.
beats.jcurve: [[a]]An alternative investment has a long life cycle with three phases. [[commit]]First, capital commitment. The manager selects investments, and capital is called. Fees and expenses are charged, but there is little income, so returns are usually negative. [[deploy]]Second, capital deployment. Money goes into construction, turnarounds, or startups. Outflows exceed inflows, and management fees keep dragging on returns. [[dist]]Third, capital distribution. If it worked, assets appreciate or generate income, investments are sold, and returns accelerate. [[pt]]This initial dip followed by a rise is the J-curve. Because of the uneven cash flows, the internal rate of return is the usual starting point.
beats.irr: [[a]]Take a private equity vehicle with this pattern of net cash flows over six years. [[out]]Money goes out in the first four years: two and a half million, four, one point seven, and a net half million. [[in]]Then it comes back: one million, three million, and twelve and a half million. [[res]]The internal rate of return, the discount rate that makes the cash flows sum to zero, is about fourteen point six percent. [[moic]]A shortcut is the multiple of invested capital: realized plus unrealized value, divided by capital invested. A fund that invests three point eight billion yen, adds one point four billion later, and sells for eight point five billion, has a multiple of one point six three. [[caveat]]But the multiple ignores timing. Doubling your money is great in two years, and much less impressive in fifteen.
beats.lever: [[a]]Leverage magnifies returns. The leveraged return equals the unleveraged return, plus borrowed funds over own capital, times the gap between the asset return and the borrowing rate. [[s1]]A hedge fund has a hundred million, and borrows fifty at four percent. If positions return eight percent, the leveraged return is ten. [[s2]]If positions lose two percent, the leveraged return is negative five. Leverage magnified the loss. [[s3]]If the asset return equals the borrowing rate, leverage adds nothing. [[risk]]Leverage helps only when assets earn more than the cost of debt, and a margin call can force the fund to sell losing positions.
beats.fair: [[a]]Valuation is a challenge when assets rarely trade. Fair value follows a three-level hierarchy. [[l1]]Level one: quoted prices in active markets, such as listed shares. [[l2]]Level two: inputs that can be observed directly or indirectly, such as an over-the-counter interest rate derivative priced by a model from market data. [[l3]]Level three: unobservable inputs, such as private equity and real estate valued with cash flow projection models. [[risk]]Level three values are mark-to-model. Valuations may stay near cost for years, smoothing returns and understating volatility. Funds heavy in level three assets deserve extra due diligence.
beats.terms: [[a]]Liquidity terms protect the fund from forced selling. [[notice]]A notice period, often thirty to ninety days, gives the manager time to sell in an orderly way. [[lock]]A lockup is a minimum holding period before withdrawals. [[gate]]A gate lets the manager limit redemptions for a time. [[fee]]A redemption fee compensates remaining investors for transaction costs. [[custom]]Fees themselves can be customized. Longer lockups can earn lower fees, and larger investors can negotiate discounts. Founders shares reward early investors with, for example, one and a half percent and ten percent in place of two and twenty. And with an either-or fee, the manager receives the greater of a low fixed fee, or a high incentive fee above a hurdle.
beats.kettle: [[a]]Now calculate net returns. Kettleside Timberland starts with a hundred million dollars, charges a one percent management fee on year-end assets, and a twenty percent performance fee. In year one, it returns thirty percent. [[ind]]If the two fees are calculated independently, the manager earns one point three million, plus six million: seven point three. Investors keep twenty-two point seven percent. [[net]]If the performance fee is calculated after the management fee, the manager earns seven point oh four million, and investors keep twenty-two point nine six. [[hurdle]]With a six percent hard hurdle, the performance fee applies only above the hurdle. Fees fall to five point eight four million, and investors keep twenty-four point one six percent.
beats.hwm: [[a]]Now add a high-water mark. After year one, investors' capital is a hundred twenty-two point seven million. [[y2]]In year two, the fund falls to a hundred ten. The manager charges only the management fee, one point one million, and investors lose eleven point two five percent. [[y3]]In year three, the fund rises to a hundred twenty-eight. The performance fee applies only to the gain above the high-water mark of a hundred twenty-two point seven, so the fee is two point three four million. Investors earn fifteen point three nine percent. [[new]]A new investor who joined at the end of year two pays on the whole gain, with no high-water mark relief. The fee is five point one million, and the return is twelve point eight five six percent. Same fund, same year, different returns.
beats.claw: [[a]]A clawback works across deals. Tenderledge invests ten million in a buyout, and ten million in an early-stage venture. [[win]]A year later, the buyout is sold for twenty-two million: a twelve million profit. Twenty percent, two point four million, is accrued for the manager, usually held in escrow. [[loss]]Two years later, the venture fails, and loses ten million. [[res]]The fund's total profit is only two million, so the performance fee is just four hundred thousand dollars. The manager must return two million of the fees it accrued.
beats.wrap: [[w1]]Alternatives are hard to appraise: uneven cash flows, leverage, level three valuations, and complex fees. [[w2]]The J-curve, and the internal rate of return, reflect the life cycle. The multiple of invested capital is simple, but ignores timing. [[w3]]Leverage adds to return only when assets earn more than the cost of debt. [[w4]]Hurdles, high-water marks and clawbacks change net returns, and can differ by investor.
beats.finish: Module two complete. Next: private capital, equity and debt.
